lesson.subject: literacy
lesson.title: A Letter from Bear
lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 3, Session 3
lesson.footer: Persuasive Writing | Year 5/6 Literacy | Week 3 Session 3

plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Level 5: VC2E5LE04 the effects of imagery (simile, metaphor, personification); VC2E5LE02 opinions on a literary text (The Last Bear); VC2E5LY10 creating persuasive texts for an audience
plan.shape: model, sort, picture, write: a model letter in role, a quick sort of imagery types, then students write their own letter as a polar bear, because a voice and a character unlock writing for reluctant writers
plan.criticalFeature: imagery shows the reader the problem so they feel it; the bear's point of view decides what the reader cares about
decisionPoints: the Simile, metaphor or personification? round
the choice check: which line helps you picture the problem?
the exit board: a new animal, a new image
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. Today the bear does all three, in its own voice.
plan.catchUp: Missed the week? Show the model letter and say: write as the bear, show the problem with a picture, ask humans to act.

studentTools: The class copy of The Last Bear
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: Three imagery types: 1 simile (like, as), 2 metaphor (is a), 3 personification (acts human)
Letter outline: Dear Humans / who I am / my problem / what I need / sign-off

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn: name the imagery, aim it at the problem, make pictures, then write your Letter from Bear.
resources.title: A Letter from Bear
resources.subtitle: Help the reader picture the problem, then ask them to act.

items.prompt: Name the imagery: simile, metaphor or personification.
rows: The ice groaned under my weight.
My den is a cave of snow.
The sea is as grey as old steel.
The sun stared down at the melting floe.
My cubs ran like snowballs down the hill.
answers: The ice groaned under my weight.
My den is a cave of snow.
The sea is as grey as old steel.
The sun stared down at the melting floe.
My cubs ran like snowballs down the hill.

example.prompt: Problem: thin ice. Image: The ice is as thin as a biscuit.
steps: Pick a picture that shows it
Check: does it show the problem?
example.answer: Yes: a thin biscuit snaps, just like the ice.

items.prompt: Problem: hunger. Which image shows it best?
options: My fur is white as snow.
items.explain: A growling belly shows hunger; the others are pretty but off-topic.

items.prompt: Kai wrote this line for his letter. Find the problem and fix it.
work: The sky was like pink candy floss.
items.answer: It's pretty, but not about the bear's problem. Fix: The ice cracked like a dropped plate.

example.answer: The sea is a warm bath where ice goes to die.

items.prompt: Turn each plain line into an image.
answers: My home melts away like ice cream in the sun.
My legs are heavy anchors after days at sea.
Your cities glow like distant stars.

steps: Who I am and my problem
Two or more images that show it
What I need you to do, and sign off
example.answer: Once, the ice was a highway. Now it is a broken jigsaw. I am asking you to...

items.prompt: Write your letter to humans as a polar bear (or a seal or Arctic fox). Use imagery, then ask them to act.
items.answer: A letter in role with two or more images aimed at the problem and a clear call to act.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: three animal voices, then a reply from a human.
resources.title: Voices of the Arctic
resources.subtitle: Every animal sees the problem differently.

example.prompt: Seal: 'The ice was my nursery. Now my pups have nowhere to rest.'
steps: Use a different image type each time
example.answer: A metaphor in a seal's voice.

items.prompt: Write one line for each animal. Use a different type of imagery each time.
answers: I crowd onto beaches like people at a sale.
The tundra whispers that winter is shrinking.

example.prompt: Dear Bear, I read your letter...
example.answer: Your broken jigsaw stays with me. Tonight, our family switches off.

items.prompt: Write a human's reply to the bear. Show you understood, promise one action, and use one image.
items.answer: A reply that echoes the bear's image and promises one specific action.

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: Supported option: picture-clue choices, a first image done and a letter frame.
resources.title: Letter from Bear Helper
resources.subtitle: A simile uses like or as. A metaphor says it IS something.

items.prompt: The ice is as thin as paper.
The sea is like a bath.

example.answer: The ice is like a sheet of paper.

rows: The ice is like a sheet of paper.
answers: The ice is like a sheet of paper.
My belly is like an empty cave.
The sun is like a heater.
items.hint: The first one is done for you.

example.answer: Once, the ice was strong. Now, it is like paper. I am asking you to save power.

items.prompt: Write your letter: Dear Humans, Once, ___. Now, ___. I am asking you to ___. From, Bear.
items.answer: A short letter in role with one image and a request.
items.hint: Use one of your images from above.

slides.notes: Open the session. One line: today the polar bear gets to write back.
Print the Worksheet for everyone (the letter is written on it), the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for those who need it.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to write a persuasive letter in a character's voice, using imagery.
successCriteria: I can write as a polar bear, using I and my.
I can use imagery to help the reader picture the bear's problem.
I can make my letter persuade humans to act.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Today you're not you. You're the bear.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: Writing as the bear is where we start.
Making the reader picture the problem is today's main goal.
notes.prep: SC1 writing in role is reachable for all; SC2 imagery that shows the problem is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 persuading humans to act is the stretch.

slides.title: If a polar bear could write to us...
lines: In The Last Bear, Bear can't tell anyone what he needs.
What would he say to humans if he could?

notes.answer: open - help me, my ice is gone, stop what you're doing
beats: SAY: Bear can't talk. But writers can give anyone a voice.
Even a polar bear.
ASK: What would Bear say to humans? One sentence.
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: give me back my ice; I'm hungry; why did you do this?
ASK: Would Bear's letter be angry, sad or hopeful?
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest, 1 angry, 2 sad, 3 hopeful... show me.
EXPECT: a mix
SAY: Today you write that letter.
trap: answers that are just about April, not Bear.
Fix: ask what does Bear need? Student answers as Bear.
notes.prep: Launch uses the novel's premise only (a stranded bear who cannot speak); no passage needed. 3 minutes.

slides.meaning: Words that paint a picture in the reader's mind.
slides.example: The ice cracked like old glass beneath my paws.

notes.answer: words that paint a picture in the reader's mind
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Imagery. Say it with me. Imagery.
SAY: Imagery paints a picture in your head.
Some of you may remember simile and metaphor from our poetry in Term 3.
ASK: Close your eyes. What do you see in the example?
10 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: thin ice, cracks spreading, a bear's paws
trap: thinking imagery means pictures on the page.
Fix: say it's pictures made of words, in your head.
notes.prep: Retrieval of Term 3 poetry devices, now used to persuade.

slides.title: Watch me write as the bear
slides.extract: Dear Humans, Once, the sea ice stretched before me like a frozen highway to the seals. Now it is a broken jigsaw, and every summer the pieces drift further apart. I swim until my legs burn. I am not asking for your pity. I am asking you to switch off, slow down and care.
highlights: switch off, slow down and care

notes.answer: simile and metaphor show the problem; the last line asks humans to act
beats: READ it aloud slowly, as the bear.
SAY: I write as I. The reader hears the bear.
POINT to like a frozen highway.
SAY: A simile. Like a highway: once the ice took him straight to food.
POINT to a broken jigsaw.
SAY: A metaphor. It IS a jigsaw, falling apart. You can see the problem.
ASK: What does the bear want humans to do? Finish my last line with me.
3 sec. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
EXPECT: switch off, slow down and care
trap: imagery that's pretty but not about the problem: the sky was like candy floss.
Fix: ask does it show what's wrong? Student points the picture at the problem.
notes.stretch: Find the rule of three in my letter.
notes.help: Use one simile: The ice is like...
notes.prep: The model. Critical feature: imagery shows the problem so the reader feels it. Original letter, not from the novel.

slides.title: Simile, metaphor or personification?
slides.pivot: look for like or as, then is a, then human actions
slides.followUp: cold call one student: what picture did you see?

items.text: The wind howled at my den all night.
My fur is a white blanket against the cold.
The ice melted like butter in a pan.
The ocean swallowed the last ice floe.
My cubs are as hungry as the empty sea.

say: Every line is in the bear's voice.
trap: Fix: ask is something non-human doing a human action? Then it's personification.
notes.stretch: Say which picture shows the problem best.
notes.help: Check for like or as first.
notes.prep: Guided sort of Term 3 imagery terms in the new persuasive context. SC2.

slides.title: Which line helps you picture the bear's problem?

options.text: The ice is melting and it is really bad for me.
options.misconception: tells the problem plainly; no picture to feel

options.text: The ice beneath my paws is cracking like a dropped plate.
I am a big white polar bear and I live in the Arctic.
options.misconception: in role, but no problem and no picture

notes.answer: B - a simile you can see and hear, aimed at the problem
beats: SAY: Three bear lines. Which one lets you see the problem?
ASK: Which line helps you picture the bear's problem?
10 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B or C.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: what's missing from C?
Less -> close eyes, read each, ask what you see, re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: B. A dropped plate: you can see it and hear it.
And it's about the problem.
trap: pointing to C because it's in the bear's voice.
Fix: ask what's the problem in C? Student finds none.
notes.prep: Decision point before writing. Under 80% means the Make it a picture round is done with a partner first.

slides.title: Make it a picture
slides.pivot: ask: what does it look like? like a...?
slides.followUp: cold call one board: which kind of imagery did you use?

items.text: Bear says: I am very hungry.
items.answer: My stomach growls like a winter storm.
items.expect: a simile, metaphor or personification about hunger

items.text: Bear says: the ice is thin.
items.answer: The ice is as thin as a sheet of paper.

items.text: Bear says: the summers are hotter.
items.answer: The sun glares down and steals my world, piece by piece.
items.expect: an image of heat or melting

say: Turn each one into a picture the reader can see.
trap: a cliche with no link: as cold as ice.
Fix: ask does it show the bear's problem? Student sharpens it.
notes.prep: Guided imagery-making on the bear's problems. SC2.

slides.title: Your Letter from Bear
slides.task: Work through your Worksheet. Finish by writing your Letter from Bear: help humans picture the problem, then ask them to act.
slides.frame: Once, ___. Now, ___. I am asking you to ___.

notes.answer: a letter in role with at least two images and a call to act
beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Be the bear. You could be a seal or an Arctic fox if you prefer.
SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Finished? Extension next. Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Ask: where's your picture? Does it show the problem?
ASK: How many images are in your letter so far?
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest... show me.
EXPECT: 2 or more
TIME 18 minutes. At 15, three volunteers read their best line in a bear voice.
trap: the letter becomes a story with no ask.
Fix: student writes the last line first: I am asking you to...
notes.stretch: Extension: three animal voices, then a human's reply.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: picture-clue choices, a first image done, a letter frame.
notes.prep: Independent creative application. Letters can go on display or be read to another class. SC2 and SC3.

slides.extendedTask: a worksheet ending in a persuasive letter written as a polar bear, with imagery and a call to act

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: Now be a sea turtle. Write one sentence to people about plastic.
Use a simile, metaphor or personification.

notes.answer: e.g. Your plastic bags drift past me like ghosts
beats: SAY: A new animal, a new problem. Show me an image.
ASK: Write one sentence as a sea turtle, with imagery.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: a simile, metaphor or personification about plastic
RECORD who writes in role with no image. Tomorrow's warm-up.
trap: Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 with a new animal and problem. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Read your best line to your partner in a bear voice. What picture did it paint?

notes.answer: open - listen for an image that shows the problem
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can use imagery to persuade?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
ASK: Read your best line in a bear voice. What did your partner picture?
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: they saw the ice breaking up
notes.prep: Self-assessment read beside the exit boards. Display the letters if there is wall space. SC2.
